facts:
Mr Ian Barnetson was engaged by Framlington in early March 2005 as its Chief Operating Officer. On 7 March 2005 Framlington’s chairman, Lord Douro, orally offered him the role at an annual salary of £172,500 with standard executive benefits. Mr Barnetson understood from that discussion that he would also receive two further significant benefits: an allotment of restricted shares in Framlington (“the Restricted Shares”) and participation in a bonus scheme comprising guaranteed and discretionary elements. He accepted the offer and began work promptly, with the orally agreed terms left to be confirmed in writing.

Mr Barnetson said that, during protracted attempts to obtain written confirmation, disputes arose—particularly about the Restricted Shares and the bonus arrangements—between him and Framlington, and especially with Lord Douro. In March 2005, at least two approaches to Lord Douro did not produce written confirmation. Around 11 April 2005 Mr Barnetson was given two draft contracts which he considered incomplete or inaccurate, notably regarding the Restricted Shares and bonus. He raised concerns at a meeting with Lord Douro two days later, and Lord Douro indicated a further draft would be prepared.

Further meetings followed. On 20 April 2005 Mr Barnetson again raised that he still had no confirmation of his employment terms and mentioned the Restricted Shares; Lord Douro again said he would deal with it. On 25 April 2005 Lord Douro gave Mr Barnetson another document said to confirm the contract terms and asked him to sign. Mr Barnetson refused initially, querying several matters including the absence of any mention of the Restricted Shares. Lord Douro reacted impatiently, threatened to withdraw the offer of appointment, remarked that they would have a difficult working relationship, and said corporate shareholders needed formal confirmation of Mr Barnetson’s role. Under that pressure, Mr Barnetson signed the document, stating he believed Lord Douro would honour what he understood had been agreed orally on 7 March 2005 and that he regarded the document as incomplete.

Mr Barnetson said further attempts at the end of April 2005 to resolve matters with Lord Douro and Mr Alain Dromer (a board member) were rebuffed. Over subsequent months he did not raise the issue again with Lord Douro because of Lord Douro’s overbearing attitude and because Mr Barnetson believed Lord Douro would honour his word. In early August 2005 Mr Barnetson mentioned the issue to the Chief Operating Officer of AXA Investment Managers (the second appellant), which was negotiating to purchase Framlington.

On 26 October 2005 Mr Barnetson wrote to Lord Douro and Mr Dromer seeking resolution. A telephone call on 27 October 2005 followed in which Mr Barnetson expressed dissatisfaction in blunt terms; Lord Douro terminated the call. On 28 October 2005 Framlington’s Chief Executive Officer, Mr Robert Kyprianou, told Mr Barnetson he would be dismissed at the end of the year and sought to discuss terms for his departure.

On 1 November 2005 Mr Barnetson gave Mr Kyprianou a sheet headed “Ian Barnetson-COO Framlington Settlement” setting out terms he would accept for early termination, including what he sought regarding the Restricted Shares and bonus for 2005 and 2006. Negotiations then took place, including: a meeting on 18 November 2005 with Ms Louise McMahon (a human resources executive) where, according to Mr Barnetson, she proposed a bonus figure he rejected and challenged his claim to the Restricted Shares, and she presented a draft compromise agreement which he refused to read and returned, saying he would deal only with Mr Kyprianou; discussions with Mr Kyprianou on 22 and 24 November 2005 including an offer of £175,000 as bonus and Mr Barnetson’s insistence on £200,000; a discussion on 1 December 2005 where Mr Kyprianou asked if Mr Barnetson would accept £200,000 for bonus if it could be agreed internally, and Mr Barnetson agreed conditionally on acceptance of his claims to Restricted Shares and further bonus; and further exchanges up to and including 20 December 2005 proposing changes to the draft compromise agreement and including an offer of £200,000 for bonus.

There was a factual dispute about whether the draft compromise agreement shown on 18 November 2005 was marked “without prejudice” and whether that was drawn to Mr Barnetson’s attention. Ms McMahon said it was and that she drew attention to it; Mr Barnetson denied any mention of “without prejudice” and said he would not have appreciated its significance. The judge at first instance found there was no evidence to support a finding that “without prejudice” was referred to at that meeting.

On 13 December 2005 Mr Barnetson wrote to Framlington threatening proceedings if the dispute was not resolved quickly. Framlington then discontinued negotiations and, by letter dated 20 December 2005, purported to terminate his employment with effect from 31 December 2005 by making payments in lieu of notice under the written contract. Mr Barnetson issued proceedings on 24 April 2006.

The appeal concerned an interlocutory evidential issue: Framlington applied to require Mr Barnetson to re-serve his first witness statement with certain passages removed on the basis that they referred to settlement negotiations said to be protected from use in evidence. The first instance judge refused the application, viewing the discussions as attempts to agree a variation of the employment contract before any dispute existed. The Court of Appeal disagreed, concluding that by late October to mid-December 2005 the parties were already at odds about Mr Barnetson’s contractual entitlements (including Restricted Shares and bonus) in the context of an intended early dismissal, and that the negotiations were conducted against the background of potential litigation if no agreement was reached. The Court of Appeal allowed Framlington’s appeal and directed amendment and re-service of the witness statement and exhibits to omit the passages in question.
claims:
In the underlying action begun on 24 April 2006, Mr Barnetson claimed damages against Framlington for wrongful dismissal from his employment as Chief Operating Officer with effect from 31 December 2005 and for other alleged breaches of his employment contract. His contract was for a fixed term until 1 April 2007, and he challenged Framlington’s early termination and the payments/terms offered.

A central part of his position, as reflected in the factual narrative and the negotiations described in his evidence, was that he was contractually entitled to additional benefits beyond salary and standard benefits—specifically an allotment of Restricted Shares and bonus entitlements (including for 2005 and 2006). He sought resolution of those matters in October 2005 and, when told he would be dismissed at year end, he set out settlement terms he would accept for early termination, including what he sought for Restricted Shares and bonus. He rejected counter-proposals he considered inadequate, insisted on higher bonus figures in negotiations, and maintained that acceptance of a bonus figure was conditional on acceptance of his claims to Restricted Shares and further bonus.

He threatened proceedings in a letter of 13 December 2005 if the dispute was not resolved.

In the interlocutory dispute that reached the Court of Appeal, Mr Barnetson resisted Framlington’s application to remove passages from his witness statement. His arguments (as summarised in the judgment) were that the communications should not be treated as protected settlement communications because, on his case, there was no relevant dispute at the time of the exchanges and the parties were discussing the terms of his departure rather than compromising litigation; alternatively, that if negotiations began on an open basis, Framlington had not signalled any change to make later communications protected; and he relied on the absence of any mention to him that the discussions were on a protected basis. He sought to keep the challenged passages in his witness statement for use in the litigation.

facts:
Mr Day, a businessman and developer, bought the freehold of a substantial residential property in Surrey in March 2008. In August 2009 he borrowed £3,000,000 from Standard Chartered (Jersey) Limited to refinance the property, secured by a mortgage/legal charge in Standard Chartered’s favour.

In October 2010 Mr Day obtained planning permission to demolish the existing house and redevelop the site as a substantial high-quality residence, but he needed further finance. In June 2011 he entered into a loan facility agreement with TIL under which TIL agreed to lend £6,600,000 to refinance existing borrowings (including paying off Standard Chartered and discharging its charge) and a further £6 million to be drawn down in tranches against architects’ certificates to fund redevelopment. Mr Day executed a first legal charge in favour of TIL and received the initial £6,600,000 tranche. About £3,000,000 of that tranche was used to repay Standard Chartered and discharge Standard Chartered’s charge. TIL later advanced further sums, bringing total advances to £7,866,782.70.

Mr Day’s evidence was that TIL’s advances were persistently and systematically late, creating risks of contractors stopping work and causing delays; he said contractors did stop and had to be replaced. He said that on 5 July 2012 TIL went into administration and no further funds were released, leaving the property half-built, exposed to the elements, and incapable of completion because he had no other funding.

Under the loan agreement Mr Day’s debt to TIL became repayable on 9 November 2012. Mr Day did not repay and accepted he lacked the financial means to do so. In January 2013 TIL appointed joint receivers over the property to market and sell it and apply proceeds to reduce the loan. The receivers appointed Savills to market the property. Mr Day took steps to oust the receivers from possession; after the receivers re-entered and changed the locks, Mr Day ousted them again and resumed possession.

In April 2013 Mr Day issued proceedings against TIL, TIL’s administrators, the receivers and others. TIL responded with a defence and counterclaim seeking, among other things, declarations validating the charge and the receivers’ appointment and authority to market the property, and an injunction restraining Mr Day from interfering with the receivers’ possession. TIL applied to strike out parts of Mr Day’s pleading based on set-off and sought summary judgment on parts of its counterclaim. For the purposes of the summary judgment application, TIL accepted Mr Day had arguable unliquidated damages claims for breach of the loan agreement that might exceed the outstanding loan, and therefore did not seek summary judgment for the outstanding loan balance.

At the summary judgment hearing Mr Day also advanced a new allegation (not previously pleaded) that he had been induced to enter into the loan and charge by fraudulent misrepresentations about TIL’s financial status and ability to perform, and that he was entitled to rescind the charge, which would invalidate the receivers’ appointment. TIL argued that even if rescission were available it would be entitled, because it had paid off Standard Chartered’s secured debt, to be treated as having security equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge to the extent of the approximately £3 million paid.

The judge struck out the pleaded set-off argument and granted summary judgment for declarations that the receivers were validly appointed and entitled to market the property, and granted an injunction restraining Mr Day from interfering with the receivers’ possession. The judge also ordered that sale proceeds above £3,002,225.51 be paid into court, leaving TIL free to apply proceeds up to £3,002,225.51 (the amount paid to discharge Standard Chartered’s loan/charge). Mr Day appealed against the order. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
claims:
Mr Day brought proceedings asserting an unliquidated claim for damages against TIL and contended that this claim could be set off against the secured loan so as to release the property from TIL’s charge and thereby invalidate the receivers’ appointment. On that basis he sought declarations that the receivers’ appointment was void and injunctions to stop all marketing of the property until further court order.

In resisting TIL’s applications, Mr Day advanced two main lines of case.

First, he relied on the set-off contention: that his unliquidated damages claim (arising from alleged breaches of the loan facility, including late advances and the cessation of funding after TIL entered administration) could be set off against the loan debt so that TIL could not enforce its security and the receivers’ appointment should be treated as invalid.

Second, he advanced a rescission case based on alleged fraudulent misrepresentations: he alleged he was induced to enter into the loan and charge by fraudulent misrepresentations made on TIL’s behalf about TIL’s solvency/financial status and its ability to comply with the loan agreement going forward. He argued that he had rescinded, or was entitled to rescind, the charge (and/or loan agreement), and that rescission would invalidate the receivers’ appointment.

On appeal, Mr Day sought to overturn the strike-out and summary judgment orders. His arguments included that TIL should not be able to rely on rights equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge unless and until it was determined that TIL had not obtained the security it bargained for; that the receivers could not be treated as properly appointed by reference to Standard Chartered’s former charge because TIL had not appointed them under that charge and the preconditions for appointment under it had not been satisfied; and that equitable principles (including “do equity” and “clean hands”) should defeat any attempt by TIL to rely on security equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge where the payment to discharge Standard Chartered was said to have been made under a facility procured by fraud and where Mr Day alleged damages exceeding the amount paid. He also maintained (while accepting the Court of Appeal was bound by existing authority) that the judge was wrong to hold that an unliquidated cross-claim could not prevent enforcement of the security.
